records.name: Gabon
records.summary: Gabon demands real caution — and on a surprising positive trajectory: after briefly criminalising same-sex intimacy in 2019, it decriminalised in 2020, and in November 2024 voters ratified a new constitution that rejected calls to criminalise homosexuality. No LGR; social conservatism; but the constitutional debate is now public and the pro-criminalisation side lost.

sources.claim: Outright International country overview (updated March 2026): Gabon criminalised same-sex intimacy in 2019 (up to 6 months and a large fine), then decriminalised in 2020 after Senate approval of repeal - sharply dividing opinion. The November 2024 constitution codified the right to respect for private life (Article 18) but retained Article 169 limiting marriage to opposite-sex couples. No legal gender recognition.

Erasing 76 Crimes (Nov 2024): Gabon's new constitution (ratified by referendum with 90%+ approval) rejected appeals to criminalise homosexuality and included protections for LGBT+ rights, while codifying a marriage definition excluding same-sex couples; civil society had pushed for criminalisation during the drafting under the transitional military regime.

US State Department 2019 Human Rights Report for Gabon: official assessment covering the year the new penal code criminalised same-sex conduct - documents the legal change and societal discrimination.

LGBTQ Nation (Dec 2019): Gabon criminalised homosexuality (up to 6 months' prison, ~$8,500 fine) - a country that never had a colonial ban; two men already arrested and had to bribe police to be released; activist Davis Mac-Iyalla: the law 'sent the LGBT community underground and created harassment'.
Washington Blade (July 2020): Gabon formally decriminalised homosexuality - the National Assembly overturned the 2019 ban, restoring the pre-2019 status where same-sex conduct was not criminal.

Gabon Review (Oct 2019, in French): analysis of the new penal code (law 042/2018 of 5 July 2019) - Article 402 classifies 'sexual relations between people of the same sex' under 'sexual assaults and attacks on morals'; recalls the 2013 controversy when two men celebrating a union were arrested and released because no law then criminalised adults.

records.name: United Kingdom
records.summary:
The United Kingdom has a documented, in-force rollback concentrated on facilities and detention that directly affects trans visitors. Bathroom and changing-room use is now directed by biological sex under the Equality watchdog's statutory code — a daily, nationwide civil restriction (the UK is the only country above 0.55 in this dataset with a nationally-legislated bathroom restriction). Since the April 2025 Supreme Court ruling, two severe-when-triggered risks apply if arrested: police forces strip-search trans women according to biological sex (with male officers), and trans women are placed in men's prisons — with documented suicide-risk litigation.

Documented trans killings have occurred (Brianna Ghey, 2023, and others). The climate is actively deteriorating via courts/EHRC-led rollback (not executive demonization — a contrast with the United States).

The UK's traveler-relevant positives are limited: no trans-specific border friction (foreign passports with X or amended markers are accepted), hate-crime law covering gender identity (theoretical recourse), no criminalisation, and functional institutions. The Gender Recognition Certificate and marriage equality — previously cited as positives — are resident-facing and do not apply to visitors.

sources.claim: BBC (June 2026): a Scottish judge ruled the Scottish Prison Service guidance allowing some trans prisoners to be housed in jails matching their gender identity unlawful - sex segregation in prisons must be based on biological sex, following the UK Supreme Court's April 2025 'definition of a woman' ruling.

BBC (Feb 2026): in the same litigation, government lawyers argued that requiring trans prisoners to be held according to sex at birth would breach human rights and create an unacceptable suicide risk; the Supreme Court ruling loomed over the case.

The Guardian (April 2025): British Transport Police amended its strip-searching policy after the Supreme Court gender ruling - trans women would be strip-searched by male officers as an 'interim position', directly affecting trans travellers on UK railways.

Police Scotland (June 2025): interim guidance on searching transgender persons and by transgender officers - searches involving removal of more than a jacket, gloves, headgear or footwear will be conducted on the basis of biological sex, following the UK Supreme Court judgment on the Equality Act.

UK Constitutional Law Association analysis (July 2026) of For Women Scotland v Scottish Ministers [2026] CSOH 59: critique of the judgment striking down the Scottish Prison Service's trans-custody policy, covering the Equality Act, Prison Rules, the Gender Recognition Act 2004 and Article 8.

BBC (Aug 2026): the EHRC's updated code of practice on single-sex spaces came into force in England, Wales and Scotland - single-sex facilities such as toilets and changing rooms should be organised based on biological sex; trans people should use gender-neutral facilities or those matching their biological sex. Applies to cafes, leisure centres, public toilets, shelters and more.

TransActual UK 'Gendered Spaces Report 2025': documents trans people's experiences of accessing gendered spaces in the UK amid the hostile post-Supreme-Court environment, alongside related research (Trans Lives 2025, healthcare reports).

JURIST (Aug 2026): UN human rights experts warned that the UK's revised Equality Act Code of Practice (statutory from 5 August 2026) risks institutionalised discrimination - it advises that single-sex services must either exclude trans women or admit men, 'effectively presenting exclusion as a means of' legal compliance.
NOTE: Not retrievable at research time (HTTP 403); the underlying document is Surrey Police's searching/biological-sex policy (FOI release).

records.name: Georgia
records.summary:
Georgia is dangerous for trans visitors — and deteriorating fast. In September 2024 parliament passed the Russia-style law “On the Protection of Family Values and Minors”: it bans legal gender recognition, transition-related healthcare, LGBT public assembly, and dissemination of LGBT information — the region's harshest legislative package outside Russia itself. One day after passage, Kesaria Abramidze, one of Georgia's best-known transgender women, was stabbed to death in her Tbilisi apartment; mourners and AP drew a direct line between the law's rhetoric and the killing.

This compounds an existing pattern: the 2021 Pride office ransacking by far-right mobs while police stood by, the foreign-agents law choking LGBT NGOs (which refuse to register and face bankruptcy), and documented police failure to protect demonstrators (Identoba v. Georgia ECtHR line of cases, still unimplemented). Georgia's visible trans community is now legally erased and physically targeted.

For a visitor: being visibly trans in Georgia now carries both statutory risk (assembly/information provisions) and elevated street-violence risk, with police as unreliable protectors.

sources.claim: BBC (Sept 2024): trans model and influencer Kesaria Abramidze, 37, one of Georgia's best-known trans women, was stabbed to death in her Tbilisi flat one day after parliament passed the sweeping anti-LGBT 'Protection of Family Values and Minors' bill (84-0). Rights groups linked the killing to the government's promotion of the law; the President called it 'horrendous'. The law bans same-sex marriage, gender-affirming surgeries, adoption by non-heterosexuals, and 'promotion' of same-sex relationships in schools.

AP (Oct 2024): 'Georgia's anti-LGBTQ+ measures raise fears of hate crimes in the conservative South Caucasus nation' — after the stabbing death of trans actress-model Kesaria Abramidze, Russia-style 'gay propaganda' laws stoke fear.

ILGA-Europe Annual Review 2025 (covering 2024) chapter on Georgia: the foreign agents law endangers LGBTI service provision (organisations refusing to register as 'foreign agents' face fines/bankruptcy); the anti-LGBTI law eroded trust, decreasing service applications; large numbers of LGBTI people are fleeing the country and seeking asylum documentation; misinformation demonising the LGBTI community is spreading.

WISG et al. report (Aug 2024) to the Council of Europe Committee of Ministers on implementation of the Identoba group of ECtHR judgments (Aghdgomelashvili and Japaridze; WISG and Others v. Georgia): ineffective investigations into police misconduct and failure to protect demonstrators from homophobic/transphobic violence; risk of statutes of limitations expiring; new regressive anti-LGBTI legislative initiatives.

IWPR Global Voices (May 2012): 'Georgian Laws Discriminate on Transgender Rights' - legal activists say the law should be changed to allow gender recognition; job applications become difficult when a person's gender identity doesn't match official paperwork - trans-specific legal barriers in Georgia.

OC Media (June 2019): Georgia's Interior Ministry declared holding Tbilisi Pride 'impossible' in the planned city-centre locations 'due to safety risks'; organisers reported pressure from an unidentified government official to cancel; far-right groups had vowed to thwart Georgia's first Pride - state obstruction of LGBT assembly.

records.name: Guernsey
records.summary:
A self-governing Crown Dependency with its own parliament, Guernsey moved briskly through the 2010s: in 2011 it aligned blood-donation rules with the metropole, ending the HIV-era ban on gay and bisexual donors; in June 2015 the states rewrote the adoption law to open adoption to same-sex couples, removing a fifty-year bar on unmarried couples; and in December 2015 the states approved same-sex marriage 37-7, rejecting civil-partnership and secular-union alternatives as insufficient, with the law itself commencing from spring 2018.

That record covers sexual orientation squarely; the position on gender identity was asserted in the earlier profile without any cited source and has been deleted, so a transgender visitor should treat legal gender recognition and trans-specific protection as unestablished here — the more notable local quirk being that, on the documented chronology, civil partnership arrived later than in the neighbouring dependency that shares the island group's institutions.

sources.claim: Guernsey Billet d'État (24 June 2015): official States of Guernsey legislative business document - includes the review of Adoption Law (p.1170) that led to same-sex couples' adoption rights.

BBC News (Dec 2015): Guernsey's States approved same-sex marriage 37-7, rejecting civil-partnership and single 'Union Civile' alternatives; legislation expected no earlier than 2017 - described by charity Liberate as 'an historic day'.

BBC News (June 2015): Guernsey law change allows same-sex couples to adopt - the 50-year-old Adoption Law had banned all unmarried couples from adopting; new law recognises civil partnerships and gives equal parental responsibility.
BBC News (Sept 2011): Guernsey to follow the UK's relaxation of blood-donor rules, allowing gay and bisexual men to donate after a 12-month deferral - ending the 1980s HIV-era ban.

records.name: Ghana
records.summary:
Ghana is dangerous for trans visitors — and narrowly avoided becoming much worse. In February 2024 parliament unanimously passed the Human Sexual Rights and Family Values Bill: up to 3 years in prison for simply identifying as LGBT, and 5 years for “promotion.” President Akufo-Addo refused to assent pending legal challenges, the Supreme Court dismissed the challenges in December 2024, and the bill lapsed when the 8th parliament dissolved — but its unanimous passage and broad public support signal the political climate, and reintroduction is expected.

Under existing law, “unnatural carnal knowledge” carries up to 3 years, and mob justice against perceived LGBT people is documented. There is no legal gender recognition and no anti-discrimination protection. Accra has a resilient underground community (LGBT+ Rights Ghana — whose 2021 office opening was raided and shut down within weeks), but nothing that can protect a visitor.

sources.claim: NOTE: Not retrievable at research time (HTTP 401); the underlying Reuters report (Feb 2024) covers Ghana's parliament passing the anti-LGBT bill.
Human Rights Watch (Mar 2024): 'Ghana: President Should Veto Anti-LGBT Bill' — urges a veto of the bill sharply increasing penalties and criminalising advocacy.

BBC (Dec 2024): Ghana's Supreme Court unanimously dismissed two legal challenges to the anti-LGBT bill (three years' imprisonment for identifying as LGBT, five for forming or funding LGBT groups), ruling the cases could not be reviewed until presidential assent. Gay sex was already punishable by up to three years. Fear and uncertainty gripped Ghana's LGBT community; the UN condemned the bill as one of Africa's most draconian.

JURIST (Feb 2024): Ghana's Parliament unanimously passed the Promotion of Proper Human Sexual Rights and Ghanaian Family Values Bill 2021, criminalising identifying as LGBTQ+ (up to 3 years) and forming or funding LGBT groups (up to 5 years); the bill proscribes 'propaganda, advocacy or promotion' of LGBTQ+ activities.

HRW report (Jan 2018) 'No Choice but to Deny Who I Am': full PDF - violence and discrimination against LGBT people in Ghana; section 104(1)(b) criminalises 'unnatural carnal knowledge' but is rarely enforced; documents mob violence, police abuse, and extortion.

HRW report page (Jan 2018): opens with Pearl's account - a lesbian woman beaten by a crowd and nearly burned in Kumasi after a police officer kicked her; Ghana criminalises same-sex conduct via a colonial-era law that is rarely enforced, but unlike some neighbours has not stiffened penalties - documents pervasive violence and discrimination.

Bachelor thesis (Diaconia University of Applied Sciences, Helsinki, 2017) by Seree Yeboa-Mensa: survey of 113 Ghanaians living in Finland on LGBT rights in Ghana - most opposed decriminalisation/legalisation, citing religio-cultural reasons and effects on children; most supported families loving and accepting LGBT members but not blessing their marriages.

freshness.fact: Ghana's 2024 anti-LGBTQ 'Human Sexuality' bill lapsed unsigned when Parliament dissolved pre-2024 election; colonial 'unnatural carnal knowledge' criminalisation persists; Pres. Mahama signalled willingness to sign a reintroduced bill

records.name: Gibraltar
records.summary:
Gibraltar legislates its own civil and criminal law as a self-governing territory on the Iberian peninsula's southern tip. Same-sex activity has been legal since 1993 with an equal age of consent since 2012; discrimination protections covering sexual orientation and gender reassignment date from 2007; civil partnerships followed in 2014, and same-sex marriage was enacted unanimously in December 2016 after a 2015 public consultation returned overwhelming support (3,490 replies from a 24,117-person electorate).

For a transgender visitor the standing gap is legal gender: no route exists to change legal gender, and there was no specific hate-crime provision denigrating a person for sexual orientation until, in July 2021, the Ministry for Justice said it would 'urgently' consider one after a wave of online homophobia during Pride month drew a rare public rebuke from the head of government. Governance of the territory is subject to regular scrutiny by the UK parliament's overseas-territories committee, which has pressed accountability standards across the portfolio.

sources.claim: UK House of Commons Foreign Affairs Committee, Seventh Report (2007-08) on Overseas Territories: governance chapter - covers good-governance expectations, corruption concerns (Turks and Caicos), and accountability issues across the territories including Gibraltar.

El País in English (Aug 2016): Gibraltar put a same-sex marriage bill before Parliament after a December 2015 popular consultation showed overwhelming support (3,490 responses of a 24,117 electorate); Chief Minister Picardo said Gibraltarians were 'polarized' on the issue.

Gibraltar Chronicle (July 2021): the Ministry for Justice will 'urgently' consider making it a specific crime to denigrate a person because of sexual orientation, after 'disgusting lurking homophobia' on social media during Pride month; Picardo: 'Homophobia... will not be tolerated here.'

Wikiwand (Wikipedia mirror): LGBTQ rights in Gibraltar - legal since 1993, equal age of consent since 2012, adoption right by Supreme Court ruling 2013, civil partnerships since 2014, same-sex marriage since Dec 2016 (passed unanimously), discrimination protections for sexual orientation and 'gender reassignment' since 2007; transgender persons not allowed to change legal gender.

freshness.fact: Legal since 1993, equal age of consent 2012, civil pacts 2014, same-sex marriage since 2016, SO+gender-reassignment protections since 2007; no legal gender recognition

records.name: Guinea
records.summary: Guinea is dangerous for trans visitors. The Penal Code criminalises same-sex conduct (3 years); a 2024 UPR stakeholder report documents violence and discrimination from both state and non-state actors; junta rule since 2021; no LGR.

sources.claim: The Advocates for Human Rights: UPR stakeholder report on Guinea (Oct 2024) covering LGBTIQ+ rights — criminalisation ('against the order of nature', up to 3 years) and social context.

US State Department 2023 Human Rights Report for Guinea: official assessment - same-sex conduct criminalised (Article 325, 'indecency' provisions); documents violence and discrimination against LGBT persons and police harassment.

The Advocates for Human Rights + Khaleem Ali joint UPR stakeholder report (Oct 2024) on LGBT+ rights in Guinea: criminalisation of consensual same-sex activity; police arbitrary arrests, harassment and extortion; a hostile and 'sometimes deadly' environment; widespread stigmatisation hinders reporting of violence.
US State Department 2011 Human Rights Report for Guinea: documents security-force torture, prison abuse, FGM, and the LGBT section noting criminalisation and societal discrimination.

freshness.fact: Criminalised: art. 274 of the 2016 Penal Code, 6 months–3 years or fine; no legal gender recognition; limited protections

records.name: Guadeloupe
records.summary:
The full French framework applies: same-sex marriage, gender-identity anti-discrimination protection, and simplified legal gender recognition — no legal penalty attaches to trans existence, and the territory's institutional life is now visible: its first dedicated LGBT+ centre opened in the main city in April 2024 under a programme establishing one in each overseas department, and local associations run twice-weekly community space, joint social programming, gay-friendly events on a dependency island, and outreach toward the tourism sector.

The documented cautions are social and custodial. A 2023 local mapping of anti-LGBT violence exists, and community organisers describe a gap between Caribbean-French LGBT life as seen from the metropole and everyday reality on the islands, where religious and communal pressure keeps many invisible outside festive settings. As elsewhere under the framework, the prison system is the weakest documented institution: the national detention watchdog found serious persistent violations of transgender prisoners' rights. For visitors: legal protection complete, community present but small, discretion still the norm.

sources.claim: BuzzFeed News feature (Jan 2018, French context): trans women in France incarcerated on the basis of their legal gender fall into a legal gray area - relevant to Guadeloupe as a French overseas region applying French law.

CGLPL opinion of 25 May 2021 on the treatment of transgender persons in places of deprivation of liberty (French context, applicable in Guadeloupe): serious violations of fundamental rights persist across places of detention, based on ~40 referrals since 2010.

Erasing 76 Crimes (Sept 2023): interview with Leïla of Guadeloupe's Secret's Out association (founded Feb 2022) - the challenge of getting community members out beyond festive events; the group runs a twice-weekly space in Pointe-à-Pitre; notes the gap between West Indian LGBT visibility in France and the situation in Guadeloupe.

BI-FWI (May 2025, in French): Guadeloupe's first LGBT+ Centre, the Maison des Diversités et de l'Inclusion, opened 24 April 2024, inaugurated by minister Aurore Bergé - part of a national programme for an LGBT+ centre in each overseas region; responds to a 2023 mapping of LGBTphobic violence by Amalgame Humani'S.
France-Antilles Guadeloupe (in French): coverage of minister Aurore Bergé's visit for the opening of the new LGBT centre to strengthen inclusion - local press reporting on the same initiative.

Erasing 76 Crimes (March 2025): Secret's Out, Queer Gang and Lovo Nova partner on social activities for Guadeloupe's LGBT community; a festive gay-friendly day on Marie-Galante; discussion of approaching the tourism committee about gay-friendly tourism.
